title: The Coin-Op Begins 1971-72
description: In 1971 the first commercial coin-operated video game arrived in bars and arcades, a space duel played on a small black-and-white screen that asked players for a quarter and gave them a few minutes of electronic novelty. A year later a far simpler game changed everything: two paddles, one bouncing square ball, and a score counter. That second game was easy to learn in seconds, hard to put down, and it turned the video game from a curiosity into a fixture beside the jukebox.
body:
In 1971 the first commercial coin-operated video game arrived in bars and arcades, a space duel played on a small black-and-white screen that asked players for a quarter and gave them a few minutes of electronic novelty. A year later a far simpler game changed everything: two paddles, one bouncing square ball, and a score counter. That second game was easy to learn in seconds, hard to put down, and it turned the video game from a curiosity into a fixture beside the jukebox.

This tribute recreates the paddle rally at the heart of that breakthrough. You guard the left wall with a short paddle while the ball bounces around the court, and every return you make adds to your score. The demo changes the original in one honest way: it is a scripted rally against the wall rather than a head-to-head match, so it shows the rhythm of the game without pretending to be the cabinet itself.

The strategy is patience. Keep the paddle near the middle of its travel, move in small steps, and let the ball come to you instead of chasing it across the court. Players who flailed lost quickly; players who waited for the return could rally for minutes, and that calm rally is what made crowds gather around the first machines.
controls: Type up/down/stay each tick to guard your wall, quit to stop.

title: The Maze Craze
description: In 1980 a maze chase game turned the arcade upside down by replacing shooting with eating. The player steered a round yellow hero through a maze, gobbling dots while four colorful ghosts patrolled the corridors and tried to cut him off. A few large flashing pellets briefly reversed the hunt, letting the hero chase the ghosts for bonus points, and that reversal became one of the most famous mechanics in all of games.
body:
In 1980 a maze chase game turned the arcade upside down by replacing shooting with eating. The player steered a round yellow hero through a maze, gobbling dots while four colorful ghosts patrolled the corridors and tried to cut him off. A few large flashing pellets briefly reversed the hunt, letting the hero chase the ghosts for bonus points, and that reversal became one of the most famous mechanics in all of games.

This tribute recreates the maze chase with a single pursuing ghost and a winding corridor map full of dots. The demo changes the original by shrinking the cast to one ghost and one maze, so the chase stays readable: eat dots, keep moving, and never let the ghost corner you. It is an original tribute inspired by the mechanics, not the game itself.

Good maze play is route planning. Clear the edges of the maze early, avoid dead ends when the ghost is near, and keep an escape corridor open behind you. The players who lasted longest treated the maze like a map to memorize, not a race to finish, and that habit turned a simple chase into a game people studied for years.
controls: Type up/down/left/right to move, quit to stop.

title: The Invader Wave
description: In 1978 rows of marching aliens descended from the top of the screen, and the arcade found its first true blockbuster. The player drove a lone cannon along the bottom, firing upward while the invaders crept lower with every step, their marching rhythm speeding up as their numbers thinned. The game kept a running high score on the cabinet, and suddenly strangers were competing for the top line.
body:
In 1978 rows of marching aliens descended from the top of the screen, and the arcade found its first true blockbuster. The player drove a lone cannon along the bottom, firing upward while the invaders crept lower with every step, their marching rhythm speeding up as their numbers thinned. The game kept a running high score on the cabinet, and suddenly strangers were competing for the top line.

This tribute recreates the fixed shooter: five columns of invaders in three rows, a cannon that slides left and right, and a shot that clears one invader at a time. The demo changes the original by giving the invaders a gentler descent, one row every third turn, so a new player can learn the column-clearing rhythm before the pressure builds.

The winning habit is column discipline. Empty one column completely before moving on, because a lone invader in a cleared column is easy to forget and hard to hit late. Work from the edges inward, keep the cannon moving between shots, and never let the lowest row drift past the middle of the screen.
controls: Type left/right/shoot to move and fire, quit to stop.

title: Vector Glow
description: Before colorful pixel graphics took over, a family of arcade machines drew their pictures with pure light: a beam tracing glowing lines on a dark screen. The most famous of these vector games put the player in a small triangular ship drifting through an asteroid field, where every rock shattered into smaller, faster fragments. The look was stark and elegant, and the motion felt like real drifting in space.
body:
Before colorful pixel graphics took over, a family of arcade machines drew their pictures with pure light: a beam tracing glowing lines on a dark screen. The most famous of these vector games put the player in a small triangular ship drifting through an asteroid field, where every rock shattered into smaller, faster fragments. The look was stark and elegant, and the motion felt like real drifting in space.

This tribute recreates vector flight: turn, thrust, and shoot across a dark field, with rocks that split when hit. The demo changes the original by parking most of its rocks in place, so a new pilot can practice lining up shots before dealing with drifting debris. It keeps the core feeling of inertia, where every thrust carries you further than you expect.

Vector pilots learn to shoot from a distance and never chase a rock. Line up, fire, and let the shot travel while you drift clear of the fragments. The players who survived longest fired sparingly, moved constantly, and treated momentum as a tool rather than a nuisance.
controls: Type thrust/left/right/shoot to fly and fire, quit to stop.

title: Jump and Climb
description: In 1981 a new kind of arcade game asked the player to climb instead of shoot. A carpenter scaled a construction site of girders and ladders while barrels rolled down toward him, and reaching the top meant rescuing someone from a giant ape. The game introduced jumping as a central skill, and its hero went on to become the most famous character in games.
body:
In 1981 a new kind of arcade game asked the player to climb instead of shoot. A carpenter scaled a construction site of girders and ladders while barrels rolled down toward him, and reaching the top meant rescuing someone from a giant ape. The game introduced jumping as a central skill, and its hero went on to become the most famous character in games.

This tribute recreates the climb as a timed run: each tick you choose to run or jump, and obstacles must be jumped over or they cost a life. The demo changes the original by flattening the girders into a single track, so the jumping rhythm is easy to read: jump just before an obstacle, land, and keep running.

The key is jumping early. A jump covers two steps, so starting the jump one step before the obstacle carries you cleanly over it. Players who jumped late clipped the obstacle; players who jumped at the last instant every time found the rhythm and cleared the whole climb without losing a life.
controls: Type jump/run each tick to clear obstacles, quit to stop.

title: The Fighting Boom
description: The mid-1980s brought the versus fighting cabinet: two martial artists facing off, a joystick and a handful of buttons, and a crowd watching the winner stay on for the next challenger. Early fighting games were simple contests of timing, with punches, kicks, and blocks, and they turned the arcade into a social arena where skill was public and rivalries formed over a single machine.
body:
The mid-1980s brought the versus fighting cabinet: two martial artists facing off, a joystick and a handful of buttons, and a crowd watching the winner stay on for the next challenger. Early fighting games were simple contests of timing, with punches, kicks, and blocks, and they turned the arcade into a social arena where skill was public and rivalries formed over a single machine.

This tribute recreates a versus bout: you pick a move each round while the computer cycles through its own pattern of attacks and blocks. The demo changes the original by showing the computer's pattern openly in the transcript, so a player can learn to read an opponent instead of guessing. Blocking cuts damage sharply, and the special move needs a few rounds to recharge.

Good fighting play is reading, not mashing. Block when the opponent is aggressive, strike when they block too much, and save the special move for a moment when it will land cleanly. The best arcade fighters were patient: they watched two rounds, found the pattern, and then took the match apart move by move.
controls: Type jab/hook/kick/special/block each round, quit to stop.

title: The Racing Cabinet
description: Racing cabinets gave the arcade its first driving seat: a steering wheel, pedals, and a road that scrolled toward the player while traffic and bends demanded constant attention. The landmark racing game of 1982 added a qualifying lap and a scenic route, and later racers added branching paths, music, and sit-down cabinets that felt like a small car in the middle of the hall.
body:
Racing cabinets gave the arcade its first driving seat: a steering wheel, pedals, and a road that scrolled toward the player while traffic and bends demanded constant attention. The landmark racing game of 1982 added a qualifying lap and a scenic route, and later racers added branching paths, music, and sit-down cabinets that felt like a small car in the middle of the hall.

This tribute recreates the race as a timed sprint: accelerate to build speed, change lanes to dodge obstacles, and finish before the rival times. The demo changes the original by turning the road into a straight measured course with three marked hazards, so the racing line is easy to study: speed is free until a hazard lane forces a decision.

The racing line matters more than raw speed. A crash at high speed stops you cold and adds a time penalty, so the fastest runs are the ones with no crashes at all. Brake early, pick a clear lane before the hazard, and accelerate through the open stretches; the clock rewards clean driving over daring driving.
controls: Type accel/brake/left/right each tick to race, quit to stop.

title: Falling Blocks
description: In 1984 a puzzle game built from falling blocks quietly became one of the most played games on Earth. Pieces of four squares dropped from the top of a well, and the player rotated and slid them into place; completing a full row cleared it and scored, while a messy stack climbed toward the top and ended the game. Its simplicity hid a deep game of planning under pressure.
body:
In 1984 a puzzle game built from falling blocks quietly became one of the most played games on Earth. Pieces of four squares dropped from the top of a well, and the player rotated and slid them into place; completing a full row cleared it and scored, while a messy stack climbed toward the top and ended the game. Its simplicity hid a deep game of planning under pressure.

This tribute recreates the falling-block well with eight pieces and a six-column board. Each piece can slide left or right, rotate, and drop, and a row only clears when every column has some height, which rewards flat, even stacking. The demo changes the original by scripting one full session, so you can watch how a flat stack clears lines and a lopsided stack stalls.

The golden rule is to keep the stack flat. Filling the lowest gaps first and avoiding tall towers on one side keeps every column useful, and a flat stack turns ordinary pieces into line clears. Players who chased dramatic clears built towers and lost; players who kept the board level lasted longest.
controls: Type left/right/rotate/drop for each falling piece, quit to stop.

title: Light-Gun Gallery
description: Light-gun cabinets turned the arcade screen into a shooting gallery: a plastic gun, targets that popped up across the scene, and a score for every clean hit. The genre peaked in the late 1980s with a military-themed cabinet that scrolled through enemy territory, and it stayed popular because aiming at a real screen felt completely different from pushing a joystick.
body:
Light-gun cabinets turned the arcade screen into a shooting gallery: a plastic gun, targets that popped up across the scene, and a score for every clean hit. The genre peaked in the late 1980s with a military-themed cabinet that scrolled through enemy territory, and it stayed popular because aiming at a real screen felt completely different from pushing a joystick.

This tribute recreates the gallery on a ten-by-ten grid: six targets appear in sequence, and each shot is a coordinate you choose. The demo changes the original by scoring near misses as hits when the shot lands one step away, which mirrors how a real light gun forgives a slightly shaky hand. Every target carries its own point value, so choosing which to prioritize matters.

Gallery shooting rewards calm aim over speed. Center the shot, take the high-value targets first, and accept that a wild shot at a distant target is worse than a careful shot at a near one. The best gallery players looked like they were barely moving, because the gun was already where it needed to be before the target appeared.
controls: Type shoot X Y to fire at each target, quit to stop.

demo.code:
import sys
PARAMS = {'targets': [[2, 3, 100], [5, 5, 150], [8, 2, 100], [4, 7, 200], [7, 8, 150], [1, 1, 50]]}
AUTO = ['shoot 2 3', 'shoot 5 6', 'shoot 8 2', 'shoot 0 0', 'shoot 7 8', 'shoot 1 1']

def auto_play():
    score, hits = 0, 0
    print("Gallery tribute: auto session")
    for i, target in enumerate(PARAMS["targets"]):
        shot = AUTO[i] if i < len(AUTO) else "shoot 0 0"
        parts = shot.split()
        sx, sy = int(parts[1]), int(parts[2])
        tx, ty, pts = target
        hit = abs(sx - tx) <= 1 and abs(sy - ty) <= 1
        if hit:
            score += pts
            hits += 1
        print("Round %d: target %s shot (%d,%d) %s score %d" % (i + 1, (tx, ty), sx, sy, "HIT" if hit else "MISS", score))
    print("FINAL SCORE: %d" % score)
    print("RESULT: HITS %d/%d" % (hits, len(PARAMS["targets"])))

def play():
    score, hits = 0, 0
    print("Gallery tribute: type 'shoot X Y' each round, or quit. Targets are on a 0-9 grid.")
    for i, target in enumerate(PARAMS["targets"]):
        print("Round %d: a target has appeared somewhere on the 0-9 grid." % (i + 1))
        got = False
        for line in sys.stdin:
            cmd = line.strip().lower()
            if cmd == "quit":
                print("FINAL SCORE: %d" % score)
                print("RESULT: HITS %d/%d" % (hits, len(PARAMS["targets"])))
                return
            parts = cmd.split()
            if len(parts) != 3 or parts[0] != "shoot":
                print("Use: shoot X Y")
                continue
            try:
                sx, sy = int(parts[1]), int(parts[2])
            except ValueError:
                print("Use numbers: shoot X Y")
                continue
            tx, ty, pts = target
            hit = abs(sx - tx) <= 1 and abs(sy - ty) <= 1
            if hit:
                score += pts
                hits += 1
            print("%s score %d" % ("HIT" if hit else "MISS", score))
            got = True
            break
        if not got:
            break
    print("FINAL SCORE: %d" % score)
    print("RESULT: HITS %d/%d" % (hits, len(PARAMS["targets"])))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "--play" in sys.argv:
        play()
    else:
        auto_play()

title: Sports on the Cabinet
description: Sports cabinets brought the stadium into the arcade, from early track-and-field button mashers to the over-the-top basketball games of the 1990s. The most beloved of them threw realism out the window: two-on-two teams, impossible dunks, and a player who caught fire after three straight baskets, with a commentator shouting over every play. Friends played shoulder to shoulder, and the cabinet kept the rivalry friendly.
body:
Sports cabinets brought the stadium into the arcade, from early track-and-field button mashers to the over-the-top basketball games of the 1990s. The most beloved of them threw realism out the window: two-on-two teams, impossible dunks, and a player who caught fire after three straight baskets, with a commentator shouting over every play. Friends played shoulder to shoulder, and the cabinet kept the rivalry friendly.

This tribute recreates the shooting contest at the heart of arcade basketball: a hoop that shifts position each turn, and a player who must aim and then shoot. The demo changes the original by turning the contest into a pattern to learn, since the hoop moves by a fixed rule each shot. Watching two or three shots reveals where the next hoop will be.

The skill here is pattern memory, not reflexes. The hoop visits positions in a steady cycle, so a player who notes the first few positions can predict the rest and score nearly every time. In the arcade, the same lesson applied to every sports cabinet: the machine had habits, and the regulars were the ones who learned them.
controls: Type aim N then shoot for each turn, quit to stop.

title: Beat and Dance
description: In 1998 a dancing game turned the arcade floor into a stage. Players stood on a pad of four arrows and stepped in time as arrows scrolled up the screen, matching the beat of fast dance music while a crowd gathered to watch. The game made the player's body the controller, and it built a scene of dancers who practiced routines the way other players practiced combos.
body:
In 1998 a dancing game turned the arcade floor into a stage. Players stood on a pad of four arrows and stepped in time as arrows scrolled up the screen, matching the beat of fast dance music while a crowd gathered to watch. The game made the player's body the controller, and it built a scene of dancers who practiced routines the way other players practiced combos.

This tribute recreates the rhythm match on a twelve-beat chart: each beat asks for one arrow key, and matching it builds a combo that multiplies the score. The demo changes the original by scripting a full session with a few honest misses, so you can see how a broken combo resets and how recovery feels. The chart is fixed, so it can be learned like a dance routine.

Rhythm play is reading ahead. Watch the next beat while you hit the current one, keep your feet or fingers relaxed, and never panic after a miss, because one missed beat costs far less than three rushed ones. Dancers who stayed loose kept their combos alive; dancers who tensed up lost the beat entirely.
controls: Type left/up/down/right on each beat, quit to stop.

demo.code:
import sys
PARAMS = {'chart': ['up', 'down', 'left', 'right', 'up', 'up', 'down', 'left', 'right', 'down', 'up', 'right']}
AUTO = ['up', 'down', 'left', 'right', 'up', 'down', 'down', 'left', 'right', 'down', 'up', 'left']

def auto_play():
    score, combo, maxcombo, hits = 0, 0, 0, 0
    print("Rhythm tribute: auto session")
    for i, key in enumerate(PARAMS["chart"]):
        pressed = AUTO[i] if i < len(AUTO) else "miss"
        hit = (pressed == key)
        if hit:
            combo += 1
            maxcombo = max(maxcombo, combo)
            score += 100 + combo * 10
            hits += 1
        else:
            combo = 0
        print("Beat %d: need %s pressed %s %s score %d" % (i + 1, key, pressed, "HIT" if hit else "MISS", score))
    print("FINAL SCORE: %d" % score)
    print("RESULT: HITS %d/%d MAX COMBO %d" % (hits, len(PARAMS["chart"]), maxcombo))

def play():
    score, combo, maxcombo, hits = 0, 0, 0, 0
    print("Rhythm tribute: type the key for each beat (left/up/down/right), or quit.")
    for i, key in enumerate(PARAMS["chart"]):
        print("Beat %d: press a key." % (i + 1))
        pressed = None
        for line in sys.stdin:
            cmd = line.strip().lower()
            if cmd == "quit":
                print("FINAL SCORE: %d" % score)
                print("RESULT: HITS %d/%d MAX COMBO %d" % (hits, len(PARAMS["chart"]), maxcombo))
                return
            pressed = cmd
            break
        hit = (pressed == key)
        if hit:
            combo += 1
            maxcombo = max(maxcombo, combo)
            score += 100 + combo * 10
            hits += 1
        else:
            combo = 0
        print("%s score %d" % ("HIT" if hit else "MISS", score))
    print("FINAL SCORE: %d" % score)
    print("RESULT: HITS %d/%d MAX COMBO %d" % (hits, len(PARAMS["chart"]), maxcombo))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if "--play" in sys.argv:
        play()
    else:
        auto_play()

title: Dungeon Crawls
description: In 1985 a four-player dungeon cabinet let friends fight through monster-filled rooms together, hunting treasure, eating food to stay alive, and pushing toward the exit while a voice warned them about danger. It was one of the first arcade games built for a team, and its dungeons, with their monsters and treasure rooms, shaped how later games thought about cooperative play.
body:
In 1985 a four-player dungeon cabinet let friends fight through monster-filled rooms together, hunting treasure, eating food to stay alive, and pushing toward the exit while a voice warned them about danger. It was one of the first arcade games built for a team, and its dungeons, with their monsters and treasure rooms, shaped how later games thought about cooperative play.

This tribute recreates the dungeon crawl as a small map: a hero, one monster, one treasure, and an exit. The demo changes the original by shrinking the party to a single hero and the dungeon to a few rooms, so the crawl's core loop is clear: find the monster, defeat it, claim the treasure, and reach the exit with health to spare. Attacking a healthy monster costs you health, so timing matters.

The crawl rewards a simple order: fight before you loot, and loot before you leave. A hero who grabs treasure first still has to pass the monster to escape, while a hero who clears the monster first walks the rest of the dungeon freely. Keep your health above half before the exit, and never fight with your back to a wall you cannot retreat from.
controls: Type up/down/left/right/attack to explore, quit to stop.

title: Scrolling Bullet Skies
description: Side-scrolling shooters filled the arcade sky in the 1980s: a lone plane or ship flying left to right, or bottom to top, while waves of enemies poured in and bullets filled the screen. The best of them balanced danger and reward, giving the player just enough firepower to survive the next wave and a reason to keep pushing into harder territory for a higher score.
body:
Side-scrolling shooters filled the arcade sky in the 1980s: a lone plane or ship flying left to right, or bottom to top, while waves of enemies poured in and bullets filled the screen. The best of them balanced danger and reward, giving the player just enough firepower to survive the next wave and a reason to keep pushing into harder territory for a higher score.

This tribute recreates the scrolling run: enemies spawn on a fixed schedule, drift toward the player, and must be shot while they are within range ahead of the ship. The demo changes the original by fixing the spawn schedule and the player's range, so the run becomes a timing puzzle: be on the enemy's row early, and fire when the target is close enough to hit.

Scrolling survival is about row discipline. Move to the enemy's row before it arrives, fire while it is still a few steps out, and never chase an enemy down the screen. The pilots who lasted longest held their ground, let the waves come to them, and treated every shot as a deliberate decision rather than a reflex.
controls: Type up/down/left/right/shoot each tick to survive, quit to stop.

title: The Arcade Hall Itself
description: Beyond any single game, the arcade hall itself was the attraction: rows of cabinets humming under neon light, the clatter of buttons, the smell of popcorn from the snack counter, and friends drifting from machine to machine looking for a challenger. The hall was a social place first and a collection of games second, and regulars knew which cabinet had the friendliest crowd and which had the toughest high score to beat.
body:
Beyond any single game, the arcade hall itself was the attraction: rows of cabinets humming under neon light, the clatter of buttons, the smell of popcorn from the snack counter, and friends drifting from machine to machine looking for a challenger. The hall was a social place first and a collection of games second, and regulars knew which cabinet had the friendliest crowd and which had the toughest high score to beat.

This tribute treats the hall floor as a maze: open lanes between cabinet rows, a wandering crowd standing in for the chasing ghost, and dots marking the stops along a night out. The demo changes a real hall by turning its floor plan into a single winding route, so one walk through the lanes visits every corner. It is a tribute to the place, not to any one game.

Walking the hall well meant the same thing as playing a maze well: plan a route, avoid the crowded corners, and keep moving so you never get boxed in. The best nights out were the ones where you saw every cabinet, played a little of each, and left with a pocket full of stories and a new rival for next weekend.
controls: Type up/down/left/right to move, quit to stop.

title: Tournaments and High Scores
description: The high-score table turned solitary play into public competition. Three initials at the top of a cabinet were a claim to fame in a neighborhood, and organized tournaments in the early 1980s gathered the best players in a room to settle, game by game, who was truly the best. Score chasing became its own sport, with practice routines, rivalries, and records that stood for years.
body:
The high-score table turned solitary play into public competition. Three initials at the top of a cabinet were a claim to fame in a neighborhood, and organized tournaments in the early 1980s gathered the best players in a room to settle, game by game, who was truly the best. Score chasing became its own sport, with practice routines, rivalries, and records that stood for years.

This tribute recreates the tournament event as a shooting contest: ten turns, a moving hoop, and a score that rewards consistency over lucky streaks. The demo changes a real tournament by scripting one player's run with a few honest misses, because tournament play was never perfect; the champions were the players whose bad shots still scored often enough.

Tournament consistency comes from routine. Aim the same way every turn, note the hoop's pattern, and treat a miss as information about the next shot rather than a failure. The players who won tournaments were rarely the flashiest; they were the steadiest, and their scores piled up one careful shot at a time.
controls: Type aim N then shoot for each turn, quit to stop.

title: The Modern Arcade
description: The modern arcade looks different from the golden-age hall, but the spirit survived: rhythm stages, card-based battlers, photo booths, prize counters, and a new generation of cabinets that mix physical play with screens. Neighborhood barcades and revival halls keep the classics alive beside the new machines, and the arcade remains a place to play together in person rather than alone at home.
body:
The modern arcade looks different from the golden-age hall, but the spirit survived: rhythm stages, card-based battlers, photo booths, prize counters, and a new generation of cabinets that mix physical play with screens. Neighborhood barcades and revival halls keep the classics alive beside the new machines, and the arcade remains a place to play together in person rather than alone at home.

This tribute recreates the modern cabinet as a falling-piece puzzle, the kind of quick, colorful game that anchors a modern hall's puzzle corner. The demo changes any single modern game by scripting a general session: slide, rotate, and drop eight pieces, and watch how the stack builds as pieces land flat or vertical. It is a tribute to the genre, not a copy of one title.

Modern puzzle play rewards the same flat-stack discipline as the classics, with one addition: plan two pieces ahead. A piece that looks useless now may complete the row the next piece sets up, and the players who thought one move ahead cleared twice as many lines as the players who only reacted to the falling piece.
controls: Type left/right/rotate/drop for each falling piece, quit to stop.
